vids.desc: In this engaging activity, students will harness the power of a light sensor to address a pressing local issue: night-time safety in poorly-lit areas of their community. Using their creativity and technical skills, participants will design and construct a light sensor device aimed at enhancing safety for pedestrians and residents during evening hours.They will learn the use of conitional statements in coding while engaging in real-world problem-solving. This activity will empower students to use their technical skills to to improve community safety, promoting a sense of agency and civic responsibility.

Which block is used for making decisions, like checking if it's dark?

opts.2: if/else block

qs.q: Why is the Forever block essential for the "Light Guard" project?

opts.1: It runs the code only one time.
opts.2: It stops the code after one check.
opts.3: It allows the code to continuously check the light level.

qs.q: If the light sensor reads exactly 20, what will the Micro:bit display?

opts.1: The LED will turn ON.
opts.2: The screen will be cleared (LED turns OFF).

qs.q: If you want the light to turn on only when it's very dark, how should you change the code?

opts.1: Change the comparison value from 20 to a higher number like 100.
opts.2: Change the comparison value from 20 to a lower number like 5.
opts.3: Replace the less than sign with a greater than sign.

vids.desc: Using radio set group and on radio received blocks, students send messages or icons between two Microbits on the simulator. Button A sends one icon, Button B sends another.

qs.q: What block is used to send a text signal from one micro:bit to another?

opts.1: radio send string block
opts.2: show icon block

opts.2: To display icons on the micro:bit
opts.3: To ensure both micro:bits can communicate on the same channel

opts.2: clear screen block

opts.1: Check if both micro:bits have the same radio set group number
opts.2: Verify if the show icon block is placed in the on start block
opts.3: Ensure the forever block is not deleted

vids.desc: Students will create the classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors. The program will use a random number to select an option on shake and display a corresponding icon on the screen, reinforcing game logic and variables.

qs.q: What is the correct sequence of actions for deleting unnecessary blocks in the Microbit App?

opts.1: Drag the onstart and Forever blocks to the left and delete them
opts.2: Select the onshake block from the input menu
opts.3: Replace the value of the random block from 10 to 3

qs.q: What does the 'onshake' block do in the Microbit project for Rock, Paper, Scissors?

opts.1: It deletes the onstart and Forever blocks from the project
opts.2: It displays the string 'Hello' when the Microbit is shaken
opts.3: It assigns a random value to the 'value' variable

qs.q: How can you represent 'Rock' in the Microbit project?

opts.1: By showing the string 'R' when the value is 1
opts.2: By displaying the string 'Hello'
opts.3: By setting the value variable to 0

qs.q: If your Microbit project is not displaying 'P' for Paper, what could be a possible solution?

opts.1: Verify the onstart block is set to 0
opts.2: Ensure the Forever block is not deleted
opts.3: Check if the comparison block correctly checks if the value is equal to 2

qs.q: What should you do if the Microbit does not show any result upon shaking?

opts.1: Verify that the onshake block contains a correctly configured random value assignment
opts.2: Delete the input menu from the project
